title: Slow News Page Abroad
statement: A news site runs its server in Frankfurt. Readers in Vietnam see page loads of about 1.2 seconds. Most of each page is the same article text and the same images for every reader. Which change helps most? Assume the team can run a content delivery network (CDN) with edge servers in Asia.
examples: Reader in Hanoi, server in Frankfurt: each request crosses the world and back
constraints: Traffic is mostly reads of the same articles
Team budget allows one main change this quarter

approaches.name: Serve images and static files from a CDN with edge servers near readers
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: About 20–50 ms to a nearby edge when it already has a copy (cache hit; approximate)
approaches.why: Most bytes are identical for every reader, so edge copies remove the long trip for most requests. Article text still comes from Frankfurt when the edge has no copy, so the content must be cached correctly.

approaches.name: Move the whole server to Vietnam
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: This shortens every request, not only the static ones, so it works. It costs more to run and makes readers in Europe slower, so it is not the first step when most content is static.

approaches.name: Buy a faster database
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: No change to the trip across the world
approaches.why: The database is not the slow part of this problem. The distance between the reader and the server is.

title: Slow Only at the Evening Peak
statement: A food-ordering API answers in about 80 ms at night but takes about 2 seconds at the 7 p.m. peak. At peak, the server's CPU is at 98%. The measured network round trip stays at 30 ms all day, and DNS answers are cached. Where should the team look first?
examples: 7 p.m.: 2,000 ms per request, CPU 98%, round trip still 30 ms
constraints: The team can investigate one area first

approaches.name: The network between users and the server
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The measured round trip is the same at night and at peak, so the network does not explain the extra 1.9 seconds.

approaches.name: The server: requests wait in a queue because its CPU is full
approaches.hint: What is busy only at peak?
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Most of the extra time is waiting for the CPU
approaches.space: Fix with more servers or cheaper requests
approaches.why: The CPU is at 98% only when it is slow. A full CPU makes requests wait their turn, so latency grows even though each request needs the same work.

approaches.name: The database, because every request reads from it
approaches.hint: The shared store behind the server
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Could add time at peak if it is also busy
approaches.space: Check its load and slow queries
approaches.why: A busy database is a common cause and worth checking next, but the 98% CPU already points at the server, so starting here is slower.

approaches.name: DNS lookups
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: DNS answers are cached, so DNS adds almost nothing, at night or at peak.

title: Capacity for Launch Day
statement: A concert ticket site expects 1.2 million visitors on launch day. Each visitor loads about 10 pages, and 80% of all visits happen in the first hour after sales open. Assume each page view is one request to the servers (images come from a CDN). Traffic within the hour is not even, so the team's planning rule is: the servers must handle twice the average rate of the first hour. What request rate should the team plan for?
examples: 1.2 million visitors × 10 pages = 12 million requests in the day
One hour = 3,600 seconds; one day ≈ 10⁵ seconds
constraints: The site must stay fast during the first hour
Planning rule: twice the first hour's average rate

approaches.name: The daily average: 12 million ÷ 10⁵ seconds, about 120 per second
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Spreading the requests over the whole day hides the first hour, when 80% of them arrive. 120 per second is far below that hour's rate.

approaches.name: The first hour's average: 80% of 12 million is 9.6 million requests in 3,600 seconds, about 2,700 per second
approaches.hint: The busy hour, but only its average
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.space: Too few servers for the busier minutes
approaches.why: This is the right first step, but it is the average of the hour. The planning rule asks for twice the average, because some minutes are busier than others.

approaches.name: Twice the first hour's average: 2 × 2,667, about 5,300 per second
approaches.label: best
approaches.space: Enough servers for the busier minutes
approaches.why: It finds the busiest hour, works out its average, and then applies the planning rule for uneven traffic within the hour.

approaches.name: Three times the first hour's average, about 8,000 per second
approaches.label: valid
approaches.space: About 1.5 times the servers the rule asks for
approaches.why: This also meets the rule, with extra room in case the visitor estimate is too low, but it costs about 50% more than needed.
